Independent Voices 16:00 BST: Badenoch really could become PM

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

CommentI never thought I would say it, but Kemi Badenoch really could become PMAs the Conservative Party conference opens in Birmingham, its leader’s fortunes have been transformed, writes John Rentoul

BookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

This time last year a wise friend predicted that Nigel Farage would stumble and that, if the Tories could find a better leader, they would be back in the game. Well, Farage has hit turbulence and the Tories have found a better leader – she is called Kemi Badenoch.

A year ago, most people thought Farage was going to be prime minister with a big majority. Seat-by-seat projections gave Reform UK a landslide. One of them (Electoral Calculus) suggested that Labour would be the sixth-largest party in the House of Commons with just 30 seats.

The same projections now suggest that, if Andy Burnham does what Badenoch predicts and calls a snap election, Labour would be the largest party in a hung parliament. He would probably continue as prime minister with the support of the Liberal Democrats and possibly a rainbow alliance of smaller parties.

More significantly, two of the four projections based on large samples in September suggest that the Conservatives would win more seats than Reform.

Even though Reform is still more popular than the Tory party, the way votes translate into seats favours the Tories, and Badenoch is much more popular than Farage. Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved dramatically, which is one in the eye for people who think that the House of Commons doesn’t matter and that Prime Minister’s Questions is a side show for nerds.

My view is that she is currently the best performer in the Commons, which gives her MPs confidence, and it reinforces her media performances outside parliament. Focus groups consistently report that voters are impressed by her, sometimes to their own surprise. “She handles herself well at the despatch box and she’s quite amusing,” said one floating voter in one of Michael Ashcroft’s groups last month. “I think she’s quite steady.” (Ashcroft, the Conservative former peer, continues to serve the cause of understanding democracy by publishing, free, the results of his opinion research.)

The Tory fightback against Reform for leadership of the right is one of the conditions for what seemed so unlikely last year – that Badenoch might actually be prime minister one day.

Last year, even those Tory MPs who admired her told me that they thought she was a transitional leader, a “Tory Neil Kinnock”, who might enable the party to survive – and therefore to lay the foundations for someone else to possibly win the election after next. But they recognised that the party itself was in a terrible state and that its brand had suffered long-term damage in the Johnson-Truss period.

My mole in the Tory shires tells me that the party organisation is largely defunct at local level – that in most places the grass roots are as dry and brown as the real grass was across most of the south-east of England this summer.

And the party struggles with the fundamental problem that it was so comprehensively rejected at the last election because it had failed on immigration and on so much else.

Every day I get press releases from the Tory party where I just read the headline and say to myself: “But you were in government when that happened.” Yesterday it was: “Conservatives will end the broken sick note system.” Then there was: “Conservatives will build 50,000 new prison places.” There will be several of these every day during the party conference.

These doubts apply with even more force to Badenoch’s big changes. To present the Tories as different from what went before, she has repudiated net zero and the European Convention on Human Rights. Her response to the Financial Times, which pointed out that these were Tory government policies until a mere two years ago, was: “The party will be doing what I want to do, because it’s my Conservative Party now.”

I think she has made two big mistakes recently. One was to appoint Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor – he was too close to the kryptonite meltdown of the Liz Truss disaster. And the other was to oppose Andy Burnham’s fiscally responsible “adjustment” to the triple-lock ratchet for uprating the state pension.

But there is time to put those right before the next election, which I do not think will be soon – although she predicted this week that Burnham would “gamble” on an election before Christmas. I assume that this was simply to galvanise her depleted troops.

What has really changed since last year is that it is possible to see how Badenoch could win the election, which will more probably be in 2028 or 2029. If Farage and Burnham both lose ground, she is most likely to be the winner.

Farage has proved himself thin-skinned, erratic and only fitfully capable of leading a united team. His support depends on a single issue, the boats.

Meanwhile, as Burnham is about to discover at the Budget, to govern is to disappoint. He has made a better start than anyone, with the possible exception of himself, expected. But support for prime ministers and governments is always more likely to go down than up.

My point in drawing attention to the state of the opinion polls a year ago is not just to note the rise of Badenoch but to argue that politics will probably change dramatically, more than once, between now and the next election. In a year’s time, the standings of the parties and their leaders could be as different from today as they are now from a year ago.

But the fundamentals remain. Badenoch is impressive. Farage is flaky. Burnham will under-deliver. I think that the chances of Badenoch becoming prime minister have been underrated.
